rows.stem: Let both \(AB'\) and \(B'A\) be defined for matrices A and B. If order of A is \(n \times m\), then the order of B is :
rows.solution: For \(AB'\) to be defined, the number of columns of \(A\) must equal the number of rows of \(B'\); for \(B'A\) to be defined, the number of columns of \(B'\) must equal the number of rows of \(A\). Let \(B\) be of order \(p \times q\), so that \(B'\) is of order \(q \times p\). Since \(A\) is \(n \times m\), the first condition gives \(m = q\) and the second gives \(p = n\). Hence \(B\) is of order \(p \times q = n \times m\), which is the option \(n \times m\).

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), then A is a/an :
rows.solution: \(A\) is a diagonal matrix, and transposing a diagonal matrix leaves it unchanged, so \(A' = A\). A matrix satisfying \(A' = A\) is symmetric, so \(A\) is a symmetric matrix. The other three descriptions fail: a scalar matrix needs all its diagonal entries equal, whereas here they are \(-1,\ 3,\ 5\); an identity matrix needs every diagonal entry to be \(1\); and a skew-symmetric matrix must have every diagonal entry \(0\), because \(a_{ii} = -a_{ii}\) forces \(a_{ii} = 0\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: The following graph is a combination of :
rows.figure: REQUIRED — the question IS the printed graph; the stem names no curve at all. The plot shows a periodic wave through the origin together with its reflection in \(y = x\), axes marked \(\pm\pi/2, \pm\pi, \pm 3\pi/2, \pm 5\pi/2\), and the line \(y = x\) drawn. Page idx 4.
rows.solution: The line \(y = x\) is drawn in the figure, and that is the clue: the two curves shown are mirror images of each other in that line, so they are a function and its inverse. Both also pass through the origin, which rules the cosine family out immediately, since \(y = \cos x\) meets the Y-axis at \(1\) and \(y = \cos^{-1}x\) is not the reflection of a curve through the origin. The wave drawn along the X-axis, crossing it at \(0,\ \pm\pi,\ \pm 2\pi\) and turning at \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2},\ \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}\), is \(y = \sin x\); the wave drawn along the Y-axis is its reflection in \(y = x\), namely \(y = \sin^{-1}x\). So the graph is a combination of \(y = \sin^{-1}x\) and \(y = \sin x\).

rows.stem: Sum of two skew-symmetric matrices of same order is always a/an :
rows.solution:
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be skew-symmetric matrices of the same order, so \(A' = -A\) and \(B' = -B\). Then
\((A + B)' = A' + B' = -A - B = -(A + B)\),
which is exactly the condition for \(A + B\) to be skew-symmetric. So the sum is always a skew-symmetric matrix. It need not be the null matrix, as \(A = B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) shows, and it can never be the identity matrix, because a skew-symmetric matrix has every diagonal entry zero.

rows.stem: \(\left[ \sec^{-1}(-\sqrt{2}) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \right]\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
Evaluate each inverse value in its own principal branch. The range of \(\sec^{-1}\) is \([0, \pi]\) with \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) excluded, and \(\sec\theta = -\sqrt{2}\) means \(\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\sec^{-1}(-\sqrt{2}) = \frac{3\pi}{4}\). Also \(\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\pi}{6}\), since \(\tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Hence the expression equals
\(\frac{3\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{9\pi - 2\pi}{12} = \frac{7\pi}{12}\),
which is the option \(\frac{7\pi}{12}\).

rows.stem: If \(f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\log(1 + ax) + \log(1 - bx)}{x}, & \text{for } x \ne 0 \\ k, & \text{for } x = 0 \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 0\), then the value of k is :
rows.solution:
For \(f\) to be continuous at \(x = 0\) we need \(k = f(0) = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\log(1 + ax) + \log(1 - bx)}{x}\). Split the limit and use the standard result \(\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\log(1 + t)}{t} = 1\):
\(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\log(1 + ax)}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\log(1 + ax)}{ax}\cdot a = a\),
\(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\log(1 - bx)}{x} = \lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\log(1 - bx)}{-bx}\cdot(-b) = -b\).
Adding, the limit is \(a - b\), so \(k = a - b\). (The minus sign comes from the \(1 - bx\) inside the second logarithm, which is what separates this from the option \(a + b\).)

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.stem: If \(\tan^{-1}(x^2 - y^2) = a\), where 'a' is a constant, then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is :
rows.solution:
Because \(a\) is a constant, take the tangent of both sides: \(x^2 - y^2 = \tan a\), and the right-hand side is itself a constant. Differentiating with respect to \(x\),
\(2x - 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{y}\).
Differentiating the inverse-tangent form directly gives the same answer: the common factor \(\frac{1}{1 + (x^2 - y^2)^2}\) is non-zero and cancels. So the derivative is \(\frac{x}{y}\). Note that the constant \(a\) cannot appear in the answer, which disposes of the two options containing it.

rows.stem: If \(y = a\cos(\log x) + b\sin(\log x)\), then \(x^2 y_2 + x y_1\) is :
rows.solution:
Differentiate once, remembering that \(\frac{d}{dx}\log x = \frac{1}{x}\):
\(y_1 = \frac{-a\sin(\log x) + b\cos(\log x)}{x}\), so that \(xy_1 = -a\sin(\log x) + b\cos(\log x)\).
Now differentiate this equation with respect to \(x\), using the product rule on the left:
\(y_1 + xy_2 = \frac{-a\cos(\log x) - b\sin(\log x)}{x} = \frac{-y}{x}\).
Multiplying throughout by \(x\) gives \(xy_1 + x^2y_2 = -y\). So \(x^2y_2 + xy_1\) is \(-y\).

rows.stem: Let \(f(x) = |x|\), \(x \in R\). Then, which of the following statements is **incorrect** ?

options.label: A
options.text: f has a minimum value at \(x = 0\).

options.label: B
options.text: f has no maximum value in R.

rows.solution: Three of the statements are correct. \(f(x) = |x|\) is continuous everywhere, in particular at \(x = 0\); it takes its least value \(0\) at \(x = 0\), so it has a minimum there; and \(|x| \to \infty\) as \(x \to \pm\infty\), so it has no maximum value on \(R\). The remaining statement fails. At \(x = 0\) the left-hand derivative is \(\lim_{h \to 0^-}\frac{|h| - 0}{h} = -1\), while the right-hand derivative is \(\lim_{h \to 0^+}\frac{|h| - 0}{h} = 1\). The two are unequal, so \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x = 0\), and that is the incorrect statement.

rows.subtopic: Integration as the Inverse of Differentiation
rows.solution:
Integrate the given derivative term by term, writing \(f'(x) = 3x^2 + 6x - 4x^{-3} + 5\):
\(f(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + \frac{2}{x^2} + 5x + C\),
since \(\int -4x^{-3}\,dx = -4\cdot\frac{x^{-2}}{-2} = 2x^{-2} = \frac{2}{x^2}\). Now impose \(f(1) = 0\):
\(1 + 3 + 2 + 5 + C = 0\), so \(C = -11\).
Hence \(f(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + \frac{2}{x^2} + 5x - 11\). Two details separate this from the look-alike options: integrating \(-\frac{4}{x^3}\) produces a PLUS sign in front of \(\frac{2}{x^2}\), and the constant is \(-11\), not \(+11\).

rows.stem: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x + 5}{(x + 6)^2}\, e^x\, dx\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
Split the numerator so that the integrand takes the standard form \(e^x\{f(x) + f'(x)\}\):
\(\frac{x + 5}{(x + 6)^2} = \frac{(x + 6) - 1}{(x + 6)^2} = \frac{1}{x + 6} - \frac{1}{(x + 6)^2}\).
Taking \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 6}\) gives \(f'(x) = -\frac{1}{(x + 6)^2}\), so the integrand is exactly \(e^x\{f(x) + f'(x)\}\), whose integral is \(e^xf(x) + C\). Hence the value is \(\frac{e^x}{x + 6} + C\). Differentiating back confirms it:
\(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{e^x}{x + 6}\right) = \frac{e^x(x + 6) - e^x}{(x + 6)^2} = \frac{(x + 5)e^x}{(x + 6)^2}\).

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem:
The order and degree of the following differential equation are, respectively :

\(-\dfrac{d^4y}{dx^4} + 2e^{dy/dx} + y^2 = 0\)
rows.solution: The ORDER is the order of the highest derivative occurring in the equation. Here that is \(\frac{d^4y}{dx^4}\), so the order is \(4\); the minus sign in front of it is only a coefficient and does not make the order negative. The DEGREE is defined only when the equation can be written as a polynomial in the derivatives. Here \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) appears in the exponent, in the term \(2e^{dy/dx}\), so the equation is not a polynomial in \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and the degree is not defined. So the order and degree are 4 and not defined respectively.

rows.stem: The solution for the differential equation \(\log\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 3x + 4y\) is :
rows.solution:
Remove the logarithm first: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{3x + 4y} = e^{3x}\cdot e^{4y}\). The variables now separate,
\(e^{-4y}\,dy = e^{3x}\,dx\).
Integrating both sides, \(-\frac{1}{4}e^{-4y} = \frac{1}{3}e^{3x} + c\). Multiplying throughout by \(-12\) clears both fractions:
\(3e^{-4y} = -4e^{3x} - 12c\), that is \(3e^{-4y} + 4e^{3x} + 12C = 0\),
which is the option \(3e^{-4y} + 4e^{3x} + 12C = 0\). Note that it is \(e^{-4y}\), not \(e^{-3y}\), because it was \(dy\) that was integrated against \(e^{-4y}\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
For a Linear Programming Problem (LPP), the given objective function is \(Z = x + 2y\). The feasible region PQRS determined by the set of constraints is shown as a shaded region in the graph.

(Note : The figure is not to scale)

\(P \equiv \left(\dfrac{3}{13},\ \dfrac{24}{13}\right)\), \(Q \equiv \left(\dfrac{3}{2},\ \dfrac{15}{4}\right)\), \(R \equiv \left(\dfrac{7}{2},\ \dfrac{3}{4}\right)\), \(S \equiv \left(\dfrac{18}{7},\ \dfrac{2}{7}\right)\)

Which of the following statements is correct ?

options.label: C
options.text: (Value of Z at P) > (Value of Z at Q)

options.label: D
options.text: (Value of Z at Q) < (Value of Z at R)

rows.figure: DECORATIVE — a shaded quadrilateral PQRS is drawn, but the paper prints all four vertices as text directly beneath it and the options quote the same coordinates, so every number needed is in the stem. Opened before deciding. Page idx 8.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
In a Linear Programming Problem (LPP), the objective function \(Z = 2x + 5y\) is to be maximised under the following constraints :

\(x + y \le 4\), \(3x + 3y \ge 18\), \(x,\ y \ge 0\)

Study the graph and select the correct option.

(Note : The figure is not to scale)

The solution of the given LPP :

options.label: A
options.text: lies in the shaded unbounded region.

options.label: D
options.text: lies in the combined region of \(\triangle\) AOB and unbounded shaded region.

rows.figure: REQUIRED — options (B) and (D) name '\(\triangle\) AOB' and 'the unbounded shaded region', and the points A, O, B and the two shaded bands exist ONLY in the printed graph. (The constraints are self-contradictory, so the answer is derivable without it — but the option TEXT is not readable without it.) Page idx 10.
rows.solution: Compare the two constraints. Dividing \(3x + 3y \ge 18\) by \(3\) turns it into \(x + y \ge 6\), while the first constraint requires \(x + y \le 4\). No point of the plane can have \(x + y\) at most \(4\) and at least \(6\) at the same time, so the two half-planes are disjoint. This is exactly what the graph shows: \(\triangle AOB\), bounded by \(x + y = 4\) with \(A(0, 4)\) and \(B(4, 0)\), is the region \(x + y \le 4\), whereas the unbounded shaded band lies on the far side of \(x + y = 6\), and the two share no point. The feasible region is therefore empty, and an LPP with an empty feasible region has nothing to maximise. So the solution of the given LPP does not exist.

rows.stem: Let \(|\vec{a}| = 5\) and \(-2 \le \lambda \le 1\). Then, the range of \(|\lambda \vec{a}|\) is :
rows.solution:
Magnitude pulls the scalar out as its modulus: \(|\lambda\vec{a}| = |\lambda|\,|\vec{a}| = 5|\lambda|\). As \(\lambda\) runs over \([-2, 1]\), the modulus \(|\lambda|\) runs over \([0, 2]\), taking the value \(0\) at \(\lambda = 0\) and its greatest value \(2\) at \(\lambda = -2\). Hence
\(|\lambda\vec{a}| = 5|\lambda|\) ranges over \([0, 10]\).
None of the four printed alternatives is \([0, 10]\). Three of them can be rejected on sight, since a magnitude is never negative, and \([5, 10]\) fails because \(\lambda = 0\) makes the magnitude \(0\). This question therefore has NO correct option, and the official CBSE marking scheme says so in as many words, directing that "1 mark for any attempt as correct answer is not given in any option".

rows.stem: The area of the region bounded by the curve \(y^2 = x\) between \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\) is :
rows.solution:
The curve \(y^2 = x\) is a parabola with vertex at the origin, opening along the positive X-axis and symmetric about that axis. For a given \(x\) between \(0\) and \(1\) the curve supplies two values, \(y = \sqrt{x}\) and \(y = -\sqrt{x}\), so the region it bounds runs between them:
\(\text{Area} = \int_0^1\left(\sqrt{x} - (-\sqrt{x})\right)dx = 2\int_0^1 x^{1/2}\,dx = 2\left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{4}{3}\).
So the area is \(\frac{4}{3}\) sq units. Taking only the upper half of the parabola would give \(\frac{2}{3}\), which is why that option is offered; but the region bounded BY THE CURVE includes both of its branches.

rows.stem: A box has 4 green, 8 blue and 3 red pens. A student picks up a pen at random, checks its colour and replaces it in the box. He repeats this process 3 times. The probability that at least one pen picked was red is :
rows.solution:
The box holds \(4 + 8 + 3 = 15\) pens, of which \(3\) are red, so on a single draw \(P(\text{red}) = \frac{3}{15} = \frac{1}{5}\) and \(P(\text{not red}) = \frac{4}{5}\). Because the pen is replaced each time, the three draws are independent and these probabilities do not change. It is far quicker to work with the complement: "at least one red" fails only when NO draw gives a red pen, so
\(P(\text{at least one red}) = 1 - P(\text{no red in three draws}) = 1 - \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^3 = 1 - \frac{64}{125} = \frac{61}{125}\).
So the probability is \(\frac{61}{125}\). The option \(\frac{64}{125}\) is the complementary event, and \(\frac{124}{125}\) would arise from mistakenly using \(\frac{1}{5}\) as the probability of "not red".

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** If \(|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}|^2 = 256\) and \(|\vec{b}| = 8\), then \(|\vec{a}| = 2\).

**Reason (R) :** \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) and \(|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\sin\theta\) and \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta\).
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Reason (R) states the two standard product formulas together with the Pythagorean identity, and all three are true. Using them,
\(|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|^2 + |\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2\sin^2\theta + |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2\cos^2\theta = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2\left(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta\right) = |\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2\).
So \(|\vec{a}|^2|\vec{b}|^2 = 256\), and with \(|\vec{b}| = 8\) this gives \(64|\vec{a}|^2 = 256\), hence \(|\vec{a}|^2 = 4\) and \(|\vec{a}| = 2\), the positive root being the only one available to a magnitude. Assertion (A) is therefore true, and the working just given IS Reason (R) applied to it. So both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Let \(f(x) = e^x\) and \(g(x) = \log x\). Then \((f + g)\,x = e^x + \log x\) where domain of \((f + g)\) is R.

**Reason (R) :** \(\text{Dom}(f + g) = \text{Dom}(f) \cap \text{Dom}(g)\).
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Reason (R) is the correct general rule: a sum of two functions is defined only where both summands are defined, so \(\text{Dom}(f + g) = \text{Dom}(f) \cap \text{Dom}(g)\). Now apply it to the given functions. \(f(x) = e^x\) is defined for every real \(x\), so \(\text{Dom}(f) = R\); but \(g(x) = \log x\) is defined only for \(x > 0\), so \(\text{Dom}(g) = (0, \infty)\). Hence
\(\text{Dom}(f + g) = R \cap (0, \infty) = (0, \infty)\), not \(R\).
The formula \((f + g)(x) = e^x + \log x\) is right, but the claim that the domain is \(R\) is wrong, so Assertion (A) is false while Reason (R) is true.

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: Find the domain of \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}(-x^2)\).
rows.solution:
The inverse sine is defined only on \([-1, 1]\), so \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}(-x^2)\) exists exactly when
\(-1 \le -x^2 \le 1\).
Now \(x^2 \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), so \(-x^2\) is never positive and the right-hand inequality \(-x^2 \le 1\) is satisfied automatically; in fact \(-1 \le -x^2 \le 0\). Only the left-hand inequality restricts \(x\):
\(-1 \le -x^2 \Rightarrow x^2 \le 1 \Rightarrow -1 \le x \le 1\).
Hence the domain of \(f\) is \([-1, 1]\).

rows.stem: Differentiate \(\sqrt{e^{\sqrt{2x}}}\) with respect to \(e^{\sqrt{2x}}\) for \(x > 0\).
rows.solution:
The question asks for the derivative of one function with RESPECT TO ANOTHER, so name them separately rather than differentiating either with respect to \(x\). Let
\(u = \sqrt{e^{\sqrt{2x}}}\) and \(v = e^{\sqrt{2x}}\).
Then \(u\) is simply \(\sqrt{v} = v^{1/2}\), a direct relation between the two, so
\(\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{1}{2}v^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{v}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{e^{\sqrt{2x}}}}\).
Equivalently, since \(\sqrt{e^{\sqrt{2x}}} = e^{\sqrt{2x}/2}\), the answer may be written \(\frac{1}{2}e^{-\sqrt{2x}/2}\). The longer route of computing \(\frac{du}{dx}\) and \(\frac{dv}{dx}\) separately and forming \(\frac{du/dx}{dv/dx}\) gives the same value, but every chain-rule factor cancels, which is exactly what the substitution shows in one line.

rows.stem: If \((x)^y = (y)^x\), then find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).
rows.solution:
Both sides carry a variable in the exponent, so take logarithms first. From \(x^y = y^x\),
\(y\log x = x\log y\).
Differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), using the product rule on each side and remembering that \(y\) is a function of \(x\):
\(\frac{y}{x} + \log x\,\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{y}\,\frac{dy}{dx} + \log y\).
Collect the \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) terms on one side and everything else on the other:
\(\left(\log x - \frac{x}{y}\right)\frac{dy}{dx} = \log y - \frac{y}{x}\).
Write each bracket over a common denominator, \(\frac{y\log x - x}{y}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x\log y - y}{x}\), and hence
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y\left(x\log y - y\right)}{x\left(y\log x - x\right)}\).

rows.stem: Determine the values of x for which \(f(x) = \dfrac{x - 4}{x + 1}\), \(x \ne -1\) is an increasing or a decreasing function.
rows.solution:
Differentiate by the quotient rule:
\(f'(x) = \frac{(x + 1)\cdot 1 - (x - 4)\cdot 1}{(x + 1)^2} = \frac{x + 1 - x + 4}{(x + 1)^2} = \frac{5}{(x + 1)^2}\).
The numerator is the positive constant \(5\) and the denominator is a square, which is positive wherever it is not zero. So \(f'(x) > 0\) at every point of the domain \(x \ne -1\). There is therefore no value of \(x\) at which \(f\) decreases: \(f\) is an increasing function throughout its domain, and there are no values of \(x\) for which it is decreasing.
One point of care about the wording. The domain is not a single interval; it is \((-\infty, -1)\) together with \((-1, \infty)\), and \(f\) is increasing on each of these separately. It is not increasing ACROSS the break at \(x = -1\): for instance \(f(-2) = \frac{-6}{-1} = 6\) while \(f(0) = \frac{-4}{1} = -4\), so the larger input gives the smaller output once the two pieces are compared. The marking scheme's phrase "increasing in its domain" is to be read as increasing on each interval of the domain.

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are position vectors of point A and point B respectively, find the position vector of point C on BA produced such that \(BC = 3BA\).
rows.solution:
"C on BA produced" means C lies on the ray from B through A, beyond A, and \(BC = 3BA\) fixes how far beyond. Working with position vectors,
\(\overrightarrow{BA} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}\), and \(\overrightarrow{BC} = 3\,\overrightarrow{BA}\),
so \(\vec{c} - \vec{b} = 3\left(\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right)\), giving
\(\vec{c} = 3\vec{a} - 3\vec{b} + \vec{b} = 3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\).
The same answer comes from the section formula, which is the route the marking scheme takes: since \(BC = 3BA\), the part \(CA = BC - BA = 2BA\), so C divides BA externally in the ratio \(3 : 2\) and
\(\vec{c} = \frac{3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}}{3 - 2} = 3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\).
So the position vector of C is \(3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\).

rows.stem: Vector \(\vec{r}\) is inclined at equal angles to the three axes x, y and z. If magnitude of \(\vec{r}\) is \(5\sqrt{3}\) units, then find \(\vec{r}\).
rows.solution:
Being inclined at equal angles to the three axes means the direction cosines of \(\vec{r}\) are all equal, say \(l = m = n\). Direction cosines always satisfy \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\), so \(3l^2 = 1\) and
\(l = m = n = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).
A unit vector equally inclined to the axes is therefore \(\frac{\hat{i}}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{\hat{j}}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{\hat{k}}{\sqrt{3}}\), and multiplying it by the given magnitude \(5\sqrt{3}\),
\(\vec{r} = 5\sqrt{3}\left(\frac{\hat{i}}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{\hat{j}}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{\hat{k}}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = 5\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\).
Taking the negative root instead gives \(\vec{r} = -5\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}\), and that is equally acceptable: the data fix the magnitude and the equality of the three angles but not the sense of the vector, and the official scheme allows both. Check: \(|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{25 + 25 + 25} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\), as required.

rows.stem: Determine if the lines \(\vec{r} = (\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}) + \lambda(3\hat{i} - \hat{j})\) and \(\vec{r} = (4\hat{i} - \hat{k}) + \mu(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{k})\) intersect with each other.
rows.solution:
Read the two lines in the form \(\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}\):
\(\vec{a_1} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b_1} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j}\); \(\vec{a_2} = 4\hat{i} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b_2} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{k}\).
Two lines that are not parallel meet exactly when they are coplanar, and the test for that is the vanishing of the scalar triple product \((\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1})\cdot\left(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\right)\), which is the numerator of the shortest-distance formula.
Here \(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j}\), and
\(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-3 - 0) - \hat{j}(9 - 0) + \hat{k}(0 + 2) = -3\hat{i} - 9\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\).
This is not the zero vector, so the lines are not parallel. Now
\(\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\right) = 3(-3) + (-1)(-9) + 0(2) = -9 + 9 + 0 = 0\).
The shortest distance between the lines is therefore zero, so the lines DO intersect each other.
A direct check confirms it: equating \(\hat{j}\) components gives \(1 - \lambda = 0\), so \(\lambda = 1\); equating \(\hat{k}\) components gives \(-1 = -1 + 3\mu\), so \(\mu = 0\); and both then give \(x = 4\). The lines meet at the point \((4, 0, -1)\).

rows.stem: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 2 \\ 12 & 16 & 8 \\ -6 & -8 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\) be two matrices. Then, find the matrix B if \(AB = C\).
rows.solution:
\(A\) is of order \(3 \times 1\) and \(C\) is of order \(3 \times 3\), so in \(AB = C\) the matrix \(B\) must be of order \(1 \times 3\); no other order makes the product defined and of the right size. Write \(B = \begin{bmatrix} x & y & z \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x & y & z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y & z \\ 4x & 4y & 4z \\ -2x & -2y & -2z \end{bmatrix}\).
Setting this equal to \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 2 \\ 12 & 16 & 8 \\ -6 & -8 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\) and comparing the first row gives
\(x = 3\), \(y = 4\), \(z = 2\).
Those values must now be consistent with the other six entries, and they are: \(4x = 12\), \(4y = 16\), \(4z = 8\), \(-2x = -6\), \(-2y = -8\), \(-2z = -4\), all of which hold. Hence
\(B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.stem: Differentiate \(y = \sin^{-1}(3x - 4x^3)\) w.r.t. x, if \(x \in \left[-\dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{1}{2}\right]\).
rows.solution:
The expression \(3x - 4x^3\) is the sine triple-angle identity in disguise, so substitute \(x = \sin t\), that is \(t = \sin^{-1}x\). Then
\(3x - 4x^3 = 3\sin t - 4\sin^3 t = \sin 3t\), so \(y = \sin^{-1}\left(\sin 3t\right)\).
The restriction on \(x\) is what makes the next step legal, and it is the whole point of the question. For \(x \in \left[-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right]\) we have \(t \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{6}\right]\), hence \(3t \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), which is exactly the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\). Therefore \(\sin^{-1}(\sin 3t) = 3t\) and
\(y = 3t = 3\sin^{-1}x\).
Differentiating, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\).
Differentiating the original form directly gives the same value by a longer route: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3 - 12x^2}{\sqrt{1 - \left(3x - 4x^3\right)^2}}\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.stem: Differentiate \(y = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 - x^2}{1 + x^2}\right)\) with respect to x, when \(x \in (0, 1)\).
rows.solution:
The expression \(\frac{1 - x^2}{1 + x^2}\) is the cosine double-angle identity in tangent form, so substitute \(x = \tan t\), that is \(t = \tan^{-1}x\). Then
\(\frac{1 - \tan^2 t}{1 + \tan^2 t} = \cos 2t\), so \(y = \cos^{-1}\left(\cos 2t\right)\).
Check the range before cancelling. For \(x \in (0, 1)\) we have \(t \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), hence \(2t \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which lies inside the principal range \([0, \pi]\) of \(\cos^{-1}\). Therefore \(\cos^{-1}(\cos 2t) = 2t\) and
\(y = 2t = 2\tan^{-1}x\).
Differentiating, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2}{1 + x^2}\).
The direct route agrees. Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1 - x^2}{1 + x^2}\right) = \frac{-4x}{(1 + x^2)^2}\) and \(1 - \left(\frac{1 - x^2}{1 + x^2}\right)^2 = \frac{4x^2}{(1 + x^2)^2}\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-1}{\frac{2x}{1 + x^2}}\cdot\frac{-4x}{(1 + x^2)^2} = \frac{2}{1 + x^2}\) for \(x > 0\).

rows.stem: A student wants to pair up natural numbers in such a way that they satisfy the equation \(2x + y = 41\), \(x,\ y \in N\). Find the domain and range of the relation. Check if the relation thus formed is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Hence, state whether it is an equivalence relation or not.
rows.solution:
The relation is \(R = \{(x, y) : 2x + y = 41,\ x, y \in N\}\). For each \(x\) the equation forces \(y = 41 - 2x\), and this is a natural number exactly when \(41 - 2x \ge 1\), that is \(x \le 20\). So
\(R = \{(1, 39), (2, 37), (3, 35), \ldots, (20, 1)\}\),
Domain \(= \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 20\}\), Range \(= \{1, 3, 5, \ldots, 39\}\), the odd numbers from \(1\) to \(39\).
REFLEXIVE? \((1, 1)\) would require \(2(1) + 1 = 41\), but the left side is \(3\). So \((1, 1) \notin R\) and R is not reflexive.
SYMMETRIC? \((1, 39) \in R\) because \(2 + 39 = 41\), but \((39, 1)\) would require \(2(39) + 1 = 41\), and the left side is \(79\). So \((39, 1) \notin R\) and R is not symmetric.
TRANSITIVE? \((11, 19) \in R\) because \(22 + 19 = 41\), and \((19, 3) \in R\) because \(38 + 3 = 41\); but \((11, 3)\) would require \(22 + 3 = 41\), and the left side is \(25\). So \((11, 3) \notin R\) and R is not transitive.
An equivalence relation must be all three, and R is none of them, so R is not an equivalence relation.

rows.stem: Show that the function \(f : N \to N\), where N is a set of natural numbers, given by \(f(n) = \begin{cases} n - 1, & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ n + 1, & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \end{cases}\) is a bijection.
rows.solution:
ONE-ONE. Suppose \(f(x) = f(y)\). If \(x\) and \(y\) are both odd the equation reads \(x + 1 = y + 1\); if both are even it reads \(x - 1 = y - 1\). Either way \(x = y\). The mixed case cannot occur: if \(x\) is odd and \(y\) is even then \(f(x) = f(y)\) reads \(x + 1 = y - 1\), that is \(x - y = -2\), which is impossible because an odd number minus an even number is odd while \(-2\) is even. Hence \(f\) is one-one.
ONTO. Take any \(y\) in the codomain \(N\). If \(y\) is odd then \(y + 1\) is even and \(f(y + 1) = (y + 1) - 1 = y\). If \(y\) is even then \(y \ge 2\), so \(y - 1\) is an odd natural number and \(f(y - 1) = (y - 1) + 1 = y\). In both cases \(y\) has a pre-image, so the range is the whole of \(N\) and \(f\) is onto.
Being one-one and onto, \(f\) is a bijection. In effect \(f\) interchanges the members of each consecutive pair, \(1 \leftrightarrow 2\), \(3 \leftrightarrow 4\), \(5 \leftrightarrow 6\), and so on, so \(f\) is its own inverse.

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Consider the Linear Programming Problem, where the objective function \(Z = (x + 4y)\) needs to be minimized subject to constraints

\(2x + y \ge 1000\)

\(x + 2y \ge 800\)

\(x,\ y \ge 0\).

Draw a neat graph of the feasible region and find the minimum value of Z.
rows.solution:
Draw the two boundary lines. \(2x + y = 1000\) passes through \((500, 0)\) and \((0, 1000)\); \(x + 2y = 800\) passes through \((800, 0)\) and \((0, 400)\). Both constraints carry \(\ge\), and \(x, y \ge 0\), so the feasible region is the part of the first quadrant lying on or above BOTH lines. It is unbounded, opening upwards and to the right.
The two lines cross where \(2x + y = 1000\) and \(x + 2y = 800\). Substituting \(y = 1000 - 2x\) into the second gives \(x + 2(1000 - 2x) = 800\), so \(-3x = -1200\), \(x = 400\) and \(y = 200\). The corner points of the region are therefore \((0, 1000)\), \((400, 200)\) and \((800, 0)\).
Evaluate \(Z = x + 4y\) at each:
at \((0, 1000)\), \(Z = 0 + 4000 = 4000\);
at \((400, 200)\), \(Z = 400 + 800 = 1200\);
at \((800, 0)\), \(Z = 800 + 0 = 800\).
The least of these is \(800\). Because the feasible region is unbounded, a corner-point value is not automatically the minimum and must be confirmed: draw the open half-plane \(x + 4y < 800\) and check whether it meets the feasible region. It has no point in common with it, so \(Z\) can never be driven below \(800\).
Hence the minimum value of \(Z\) is \(800\), attained at the corner \((800, 0)\).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the distance of the point \(P(2,\ 4,\ -1)\) from the line \(\dfrac{x + 5}{1} = \dfrac{y + 3}{4} = \dfrac{z - 6}{-9}\).
rows.solution:
Use the distance of a point from a line, \(d = \frac{\left|\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \times \vec{b}\right|}{\left|\vec{b}\right|}\), where \(\vec{a_1}\) is any point on the line, \(\vec{b}\) is its direction and \(\vec{a_2}\) is the given point.
Reading the line \(\frac{x + 5}{1} = \frac{y + 3}{4} = \frac{z - 6}{-9}\), a point on it is \((-5, -3, 6)\) and its direction is \((1, 4, -9)\). So
\(\vec{a_1} = -5\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 9\hat{k}\), \(\vec{a_2} = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - \hat{k}\),
\(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = 7\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}\),
\(\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 7 & 7 & -7 \\ 1 & 4 & -9 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-63 + 28) - \hat{j}(-63 + 7) + \hat{k}(28 - 7) = -35\hat{i} + 56\hat{j} + 21\hat{k}\).
Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{1225 + 3136 + 441} = \sqrt{4802} = 49\sqrt{2}\), and \(\left|\vec{b}\right| = \sqrt{1 + 16 + 81} = \sqrt{98} = 7\sqrt{2}\). Hence
\(d = \frac{49\sqrt{2}}{7\sqrt{2}} = 7\).
So the distance of \(P(2, 4, -1)\) from the given line is \(7\) units.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Let the position vectors of the points A, B and C be \(3\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\), \(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) and \(\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\) respectively. Find the vector and cartesian equations of the line passing through A and parallel to line BC.
rows.solution:
The required line passes through A and is parallel to BC, so BC supplies the direction while A supplies the point. From the given position vectors, \(A = (3, -1, -2)\), \(B = (1, 2, -1)\) and \(C = (1, 5, 3)\), so
\(\overrightarrow{BC} = (1 - 1)\hat{i} + (5 - 2)\hat{j} + \left(3 - (-1)\right)\hat{k} = 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\).
The vector equation of the line through A with this direction is
\(\vec{r} = \left(3\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\right) + \mu\left(3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\right)\),
and, comparing components, its cartesian equation is
\(\frac{x - 3}{0} = \frac{y + 1}{3} = \frac{z + 2}{4}\).
The zero denominator is the standard convention for a direction with no \(x\)-component; it is not a division but a record that \(x - 3 = 0\) at every point, so the line lies wholly in the plane \(x = 3\).

rows.stem:
A person is Head of two independent selection committees I and II. If the probability of making a wrong selection in committee I is \(0{\cdot}03\) and that in committee II is \(0{\cdot}01\), then find the probability that the person makes the correct decision of selection :

(i) in both committees

(ii) in only one committee
rows.solution:
The two committees are independent, and within each committee "wrong" and "correct" are complementary, so
\(P(\text{correct in I}) = 1 - 0\cdot03 = 0\cdot97\) and \(P(\text{wrong in I}) = 0\cdot03\),
\(P(\text{correct in II}) = 1 - 0\cdot01 = 0\cdot99\) and \(P(\text{wrong in II}) = 0\cdot01\).
(i) A correct decision in BOTH committees is the intersection of two independent events, so the probabilities multiply:
\(P = 0\cdot97 \times 0\cdot99 = 0\cdot9603\).
(ii) A correct decision in ONLY ONE committee splits into two mutually exclusive cases, correct in I but wrong in II, or wrong in I but correct in II. Adding them,
\(P = 0\cdot97 \times 0\cdot01 + 0\cdot03 \times 0\cdot99 = 0\cdot0097 + 0\cdot0297 = 0\cdot0394\).
So the required probabilities are \(0\cdot9603\) for both committees and \(0\cdot0394\) for exactly one.

rows.stem:
Find :

\(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x^2 + 1}{(x - 1)^2 (x + 3)}\, dx\)
rows.solution:
The denominator has a REPEATED linear factor \((x - 1)^2\) and a distinct linear factor \((x + 3)\), so the partial-fraction form needs three terms, one for each power of the repeated factor:
\(\frac{x^2 + 1}{(x - 1)^2(x + 3)} = \frac{A}{x - 1} + \frac{B}{(x - 1)^2} + \frac{C}{x + 3}\).
Multiplying through by \((x - 1)^2(x + 3)\),
\(x^2 + 1 = A(x - 1)(x + 3) + B(x + 3) + C(x - 1)^2\).
Put \(x = 1\): \(2 = 4B\), so \(B = \frac{1}{2}\).
Put \(x = -3\): \(10 = 16C\), so \(C = \frac{5}{8}\).
Compare the coefficients of \(x^2\): \(1 = A + C\), so \(A = 1 - \frac{5}{8} = \frac{3}{8}\).
Hence, writing \(K\) for the constant of integration to avoid a clash with the letter \(C\) used above,
\(I = \frac{3}{8}\int\frac{dx}{x - 1} + \frac{1}{2}\int\frac{dx}{(x - 1)^2} + \frac{5}{8}\int\frac{dx}{x + 3}\).
The first and third integrals are logarithms; the middle one is a power, \(\int(x - 1)^{-2}dx = -\frac{1}{x - 1}\). Therefore
\(I = \frac{3}{8}\log|x - 1| - \frac{1}{2(x - 1)} + \frac{5}{8}\log|x + 3| + K\).

rows.stem:
Evaluate :

\(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{x}{\sin x + \cos x}\, dx\)
rows.solution:
Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{x}{\sin x + \cos x}dx\). The numerator alone is awkward, so use the property \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Because \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cos x\) and \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \sin x\), the DENOMINATOR is unchanged and only the numerator moves:
\(I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\frac{\pi}{2} - x}{\cos x + \sin x}dx\).
Adding the two expressions for \(I\), the \(x\) terms cancel and the difficulty disappears:
\(2I = \frac{\pi}{2}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{\sin x + \cos x}\).
Now convert the denominator to a single sine: \(\sin x + \cos x = \sqrt{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin x + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos x\right) = \sqrt{2}\sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\). So
\(2I = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\operatorname{cosec}\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)dx = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\Big[\log\left|\operatorname{cosec}\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \cot\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|\Big]_0^{\pi/2}\).
At the upper limit the argument is \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\), where \(\operatorname{cosec} = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\cot = -1\), giving \(\sqrt{2} + 1\). At the lower limit the argument is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), where \(\operatorname{cosec} = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\cot = 1\), giving \(\sqrt{2} - 1\). Hence
\(2I = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{2} + 1}{\sqrt{2} - 1}\right)\), and so \(I = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{2}}\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{2} + 1}{\sqrt{2} - 1}\right)\).

rows.stem: Draw a rough sketch for the curve \(y = 2 + |x + 1|\). Using integration, find the area of the region bounded by the curve \(y = 2 + |x + 1|\), \(x = -4\), \(x = 3\) and \(y = 0\).
rows.solution:
THE SKETCH. \(y = 2 + |x + 1|\) is a V-shaped graph with its vertex where the modulus vanishes, at \((-1, 2)\). Splitting the modulus,
for \(x < -1\), \(y = 2 - (x + 1) = 1 - x\), a line of slope \(-1\);
for \(x \ge -1\), \(y = 2 + (x + 1) = 3 + x\), a line of slope \(+1\).
The V opens upwards from \((-1, 2)\), passing through \((-4, 5)\) on the left arm and \((3, 6)\) on the right arm. Its least value is \(2\), so the whole graph lies above the x-axis and the region bounded by the curve, the lines \(x = -4\) and \(x = 3\), and \(y = 0\) is simply the area under the V between those two verticals.
THE AREA. The formula for \(y\) changes at the vertex, so the integral must be split there:
\(\text{Area} = \displaystyle\int_{-4}^{-1}\left(2 + |x + 1|\right)dx + \int_{-1}^{3}\left(2 + |x + 1|\right)dx = \int_{-4}^{-1}(1 - x)\,dx + \int_{-1}^{3}(3 + x)\,dx\).
First piece: \(\displaystyle\int_{-4}^{-1}(1 - x)\,dx = \left[-\frac{(1 - x)^2}{2}\right]_{-4}^{-1} = -\frac{4}{2} + \frac{25}{2} = \frac{21}{2}\).
Second piece: \(\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{3}(3 + x)\,dx = \left[\frac{(3 + x)^2}{2}\right]_{-1}^{3} = \frac{36}{2} - \frac{4}{2} = 16\).
Hence the required area is \(\frac{21}{2} + 16 = \frac{53}{2}\) square units.
A quick check without calculus: the region is a trapezium with parallel sides \(5\) and \(2\) and width \(3\), plus a trapezium with parallel sides \(2\) and \(6\) and width \(4\), giving \(\frac{1}{2}(5 + 2)(3) + \frac{1}{2}(2 + 6)(4) = \frac{21}{2} + 16 = \frac{53}{2}\).

rows.stem: Solve the differential equation : \(x^2 y\, dx - (x^3 + y^3)\, dy = 0\).
rows.solution:
Rearrange the equation as \(x^2y\,dx = (x^3 + y^3)dy\), so that
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2y}{x^3 + y^3}\).
Every term on the right has total degree \(3\) in \(x\) and \(y\), so the equation is HOMOGENEOUS. Put \(y = vx\), which gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\). Then
\(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{x^2(vx)}{x^3 + v^3x^3} = \frac{vx^3}{x^3\left(1 + v^3\right)} = \frac{v}{1 + v^3}\),
and therefore
\(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v}{1 + v^3} - v = \frac{v - v\left(1 + v^3\right)}{1 + v^3} = \frac{-v^4}{1 + v^3}\).
The variables now separate:
\(\frac{1 + v^3}{v^4}dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\), that is \(\left(\frac{1}{v^4} + \frac{1}{v}\right)dv = -\frac{dx}{x}\).
Integrating both sides,
\(-\frac{1}{3v^3} + \log|v| = -\log|x| + C\).
Finally restore \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), so that \(\frac{1}{v^3} = \frac{x^3}{y^3}\) and \(\log|v| = \log|y| - \log|x|\):
\(-\frac{x^3}{3y^3} + \log|y| - \log|x| = -\log|x| + C\).
The two \(\log|x|\) terms cancel, and the solution is
\(-\frac{x^3}{3y^3} + \log|y| = C\).

rows.stem: Solve the differential equation \((1 + x^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2xy - 4x^2 = 0\) subject to initial condition \(y(0) = 0\).
rows.solution:
Put the equation into the standard linear form first. Dividing \((1 + x^2)\frac{dy}{dx} + 2xy - 4x^2 = 0\) throughout by \(1 + x^2\),
\(\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}\,y = \frac{4x^2}{1 + x^2}\),
which is linear in \(y\) with \(P(x) = \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}\) and \(Q(x) = \frac{4x^2}{1 + x^2}\). The integrating factor is
\(\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{\int\frac{2x}{1 + x^2}dx} = e^{\log\left(1 + x^2\right)} = 1 + x^2\),
the integral being immediate because the numerator \(2x\) is exactly the derivative of the denominator \(1 + x^2\).
Multiplying through by the integrating factor makes the left-hand side the derivative of \(y \times \text{I.F.}\), so
\(y\left(1 + x^2\right) = \int\frac{4x^2}{1 + x^2}\left(1 + x^2\right)dx = \int 4x^2\,dx = \frac{4x^3}{3} + C\).
(The cancellation of \(1 + x^2\) is why the right-hand side was chosen as it was; note also that the original equation is already exact, since its left side is \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[y(1 + x^2)\right]\).)
Now impose the initial condition \(y(0) = 0\). Substituting \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) gives \(0 = 0 + C\), so \(C = 0\), and the required solution is
\(y\left(1 + x^2\right) = \frac{4x^3}{3}\), that is \(y = \frac{4x^3}{3\left(1 + x^2\right)}\).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Let the polished side of the mirror be along the line \(\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{1 - y}{-2} = \dfrac{2z - 4}{6}\). A point \(P(1,\ 6,\ 3)\), some distance away from the mirror, has its image formed behind the mirror. Find the coordinates of the image point and the distance between the point P and its image.
rows.solution:
First tidy the equation of the mirror line into standard symmetric form. Writing \(\frac{1 - y}{-2} = \frac{y - 1}{2}\) and \(\frac{2z - 4}{6} = \frac{2(z - 2)}{6} = \frac{z - 2}{3}\), the line becomes
\(\frac{x}{1} = \frac{y - 1}{2} = \frac{z - 2}{3}\),
so it passes through \((0, 1, 2)\) and has direction ratios \(\langle 1, 2, 3\rangle\). Doing this first matters: read carelessly, the printed form would give the wrong direction ratios and the wrong denominators.
FOOT OF THE PERPENDICULAR. A general point of the line is \(M = (\lambda,\ 2\lambda + 1,\ 3\lambda + 2)\). With \(P(1, 6, 3)\),
\(\overrightarrow{PM} = \langle \lambda - 1,\ 2\lambda - 5,\ 3\lambda - 1\rangle\).
Since \(PM\) is perpendicular to the mirror line, its dot product with \(\langle 1, 2, 3\rangle\) is zero:
\((\lambda - 1)(1) + (2\lambda - 5)(2) + (3\lambda - 1)(3) = 0\),
\(\lambda - 1 + 4\lambda - 10 + 9\lambda - 3 = 0\), so \(14\lambda = 14\) and \(\lambda = 1\).
Hence the foot of the perpendicular is \(M = (1, 3, 5)\).
THE IMAGE. In a plane mirror the image is the reflection of the object in the mirror line, so \(M\) is the MIDPOINT of \(PP'\). Writing \(P' = (x', y', z')\),
\(\frac{x' + 1}{2} = 1\), \(\frac{y' + 6}{2} = 3\), \(\frac{z' + 3}{2} = 5\),
which give \(x' = 1\), \(y' = 0\), \(z' = 7\). So the image point is \(P'(1, 0, 7)\).
THE DISTANCE.
\(PP' = \sqrt{(1 - 1)^2 + (0 - 6)^2 + (7 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{0 + 36 + 16} = \sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13}\).
So the image is \((1, 0, 7)\) and the distance between P and its image is \(2\sqrt{13}\) units. As a check, that distance should be twice \(PM\), and \(PM = \sqrt{0 + 9 + 4} = \sqrt{13}\), which it is.

rows.stem: Form the equations required to solve the problem of finding the price of each item, and express it in the matrix form \(AX = B\).
rows.context:
Three students, Neha, Rani and Sam go to a market to purchase stationery items. Neha buys 4 pens, 3 notepads and 2 erasers and pays ₹ 60. Rani buys 2 pens, 4 notepads and 6 erasers for ₹ 90. Sam pays ₹ 70 for 6 pens, 2 notepads and 3 erasers.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Let the price of one pen, one notepad and one eraser be \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) rupees respectively. Reading off the three purchases in turn,
Neha: \(4x + 3y + 2z = 60\),
Rani: \(2x + 4y + 6z = 90\),
Sam: \(6x + 2y + 3z = 70\).
Collecting the coefficients as a matrix, the system in the form \(AX = B\) is
\(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 60 \\ 90 \\ 70 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: Find \(|A|\) and confirm if it is possible to find \(A^{-1}\).
rows.context:
Three students, Neha, Rani and Sam go to a market to purchase stationery items. Neha buys 4 pens, 3 notepads and 2 erasers and pays ₹ 60. Rani buys 2 pens, 4 notepads and 6 erasers for ₹ 90. Sam pays ₹ 70 for 6 pens, 2 notepads and 3 erasers.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Expand the determinant along the first row:
\(|A| = 4\left(4 \times 3 - 6 \times 2\right) - 3\left(2 \times 3 - 6 \times 6\right) + 2\left(2 \times 2 - 4 \times 6\right)\)
\(= 4(12 - 12) - 3(6 - 36) + 2(4 - 24) = 4(0) - 3(-30) + 2(-20) = 0 + 90 - 40 = 50\).
Since \(|A| = 50 \ne 0\), the matrix A is non-singular. So yes, it IS possible to find \(A^{-1}\), and the system consequently has a unique solution.

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: Find \(A^{-1}\), if possible, and write the formula to find X.
rows.context:
Three students, Neha, Rani and Sam go to a market to purchase stationery items. Neha buys 4 pens, 3 notepads and 2 erasers and pays ₹ 60. Rani buys 2 pens, 4 notepads and 6 erasers for ₹ 90. Sam pays ₹ 70 for 6 pens, 2 notepads and 3 erasers.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Since \(|A| = 50 \ne 0\), the inverse exists and is given by \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj}(A)\).
The cofactors of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) are
\(A_{11} = 12 - 12 = 0\), \(A_{12} = -(6 - 36) = 30\), \(A_{13} = 4 - 24 = -20\),
\(A_{21} = -(9 - 4) = -5\), \(A_{22} = 12 - 12 = 0\), \(A_{23} = -(8 - 18) = 10\),
\(A_{31} = 18 - 8 = 10\), \(A_{32} = -(24 - 4) = -20\), \(A_{33} = 16 - 6 = 10\).
The adjoint is the TRANSPOSE of the matrix of cofactors, so
\(\operatorname{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -5 & 10 \\ 30 & 0 & -20 \\ -20 & 10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\), and hence \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -5 & 10 \\ 30 & 0 & -20 \\ -20 & 10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\).
Since \(AX = B\), multiplying on the left by \(A^{-1}\) gives the formula for X:
\(X = A^{-1}B\).
(Carrying it out, though the question stops at the formula, gives \(X = \frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix} 250 \\ 400 \\ 400 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 8 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}\), so a pen costs \(5\) rupees and a notepad and an eraser \(8\) rupees each, which satisfies all three original equations.)

rows.stem: Find \(A^2 - 8I\), where I is an identity matrix.
rows.context:
Three students, Neha, Rani and Sam go to a market to purchase stationery items. Neha buys 4 pens, 3 notepads and 2 erasers and pays ₹ 60. Rani buys 2 pens, 4 notepads and 6 erasers for ₹ 90. Sam pays ₹ 70 for 6 pens, 2 notepads and 3 erasers.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
First compute \(A^2 = A \times A\), taking each entry as a row of the first matrix against a column of the second:
\(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 34 & 28 & 32 \\ 52 & 34 & 46 \\ 46 & 32 & 33 \end{bmatrix}\),
where, for instance, the leading entry is \(4(4) + 3(2) + 2(6) = 16 + 6 + 12 = 34\) and the last is \(6(2) + 2(6) + 3(3) = 12 + 12 + 9 = 33\).
Now \(8I = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\), so subtracting it changes only the three diagonal entries:
\(A^2 - 8I = \begin{bmatrix} 34 - 8 & 28 & 32 \\ 52 & 34 - 8 & 46 \\ 46 & 32 & 33 - 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 26 & 28 & 32 \\ 52 & 26 & 46 \\ 46 & 32 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.stem: Express the distance (y) between the wall and foot of the ladder in terms of ‘h’ and height (x) on the wall at a certain instant. Also, write an expression in terms of h and x for the area (A) of the right triangle, as seen from the side by an observer.
rows.context:
A ladder of fixed length ‘h’ is to be placed along the wall such that it is free to move along the height of the wall.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE — a clip-art picture of a ladder leaning on a wall beside a tree. No length, angle or label is marked on it; every quantity ('h', x, y) is defined in the stem text. Opened before deciding. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right-angled triangle in which the ladder is the hypotenuse, of fixed length \(h\). With \(x\) the height reached on the wall and \(y\) the distance of the foot of the ladder from the wall, Pythagoras gives \(x^2 + y^2 = h^2\), so
\(y = \sqrt{h^2 - x^2}\).
The area of a right triangle is half the product of the two perpendicular sides, which here are \(x\) and \(y\). Hence
\(A = \frac{1}{2}xy = \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}\).

rows.stem: Find the derivative of the area (A) with respect to the height on the wall (x), and find its critical point.
rows.context:
A ladder of fixed length ‘h’ is to be placed along the wall such that it is free to move along the height of the wall.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Differentiate \(A = \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}\) with respect to \(x\) by the product rule, remembering that \(h\) is a CONSTANT (the ladder does not change length):
\(\frac{dA}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{h^2 - x^2} + \frac{1}{2}x\cdot\frac{-x}{\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\left(h^2 - x^2\right) - x^2}{\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}} = \frac{h^2 - 2x^2}{2\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}}\).
A critical point occurs where \(\frac{dA}{dx} = 0\), which needs the numerator to vanish: \(h^2 - 2x^2 = 0\), so \(x^2 = \frac{h^2}{2}\) and
\(x = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\),
taking the positive root because \(x\) is a height.

rows.stem: Show that the area (A) of the right triangle is maximum at the critical point.
rows.context:
A ladder of fixed length ‘h’ is to be placed along the wall such that it is free to move along the height of the wall.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
From part (ii), \(\frac{dA}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{h^2 - 2x^2}{\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}}\), with the critical point at \(x = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\). Differentiate again by the quotient rule:
\(\frac{d^2A}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{(-4x)\sqrt{h^2 - x^2} - \left(h^2 - 2x^2\right)\cdot\frac{-x}{\sqrt{h^2 - x^2}}}{h^2 - x^2}\).
Now evaluate at \(x = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\). The factor \(h^2 - 2x^2\) is exactly zero there, so the entire second term of the numerator vanishes and only the first survives. Also \(h^2 - x^2 = h^2 - \frac{h^2}{2} = \frac{h^2}{2}\), so \(\sqrt{h^2 - x^2} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\), and
\(\frac{d^2A}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{-4\cdot\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{h^2}{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{-2h^2}{\frac{h^2}{2}} = \frac{1}{2}(-4) = -2\).
This is negative (for any \(h > 0\)), so by the second-derivative test the area A is a MAXIMUM at the critical point \(x = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\), as required.
The maximum area itself is \(A = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{h^2}{4}\), attained when \(x = y = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}\), that is when the ladder cuts off equal lengths on the wall and on the ground.

rows.stem: If the foot of the ladder whose length is 5 m, is being pulled towards the wall such that the rate of decrease of distance (y) is 2 m/s, then at what rate is the height on the wall (x) increasing, when the foot of the ladder is 3 m away from the wall ?
rows.context:
A ladder of fixed length ‘h’ is to be placed along the wall such that it is free to move along the height of the wall.

Based upon the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Here the ladder has length \(h = 5\), so the relation of part (i) becomes
\(x^2 + y^2 = 25\), that is \(y^2 = 25 - x^2\).
When the foot of the ladder is \(3\) m from the wall, \(y = 3\) and \(x = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4\).
The foot is being pulled TOWARDS the wall, so \(y\) is decreasing, and a rate of decrease of \(2\) m/s means \(\frac{dy}{dt} = -2\).
Differentiate \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\) with respect to time \(t\):
\(2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0\), so \(2y\frac{dy}{dt} = -2x\frac{dx}{dt}\).
Substituting \(x = 4\), \(y = 3\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = -2\):
\(2(3)(-2) = -2(4)\frac{dx}{dt}\), so \(-12 = -8\frac{dx}{dt}\) and \(\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{12}{8} = 1\cdot5\).
The sign is positive, which confirms that \(x\) is increasing. So the height on the wall is increasing at the rate of \(1\cdot5\) m/s.

rows.stem: Find the probability that it was defective.
rows.context:
A shop selling electronic items sells smartphones of only three reputed companies A, B and C because chances of their manufacturing a defective smartphone are only 5%, 4% and 2% respectively. In his inventory he has 25% smartphones from company A, 35% smartphones from company B and 40% smartphones from company C.

A person buys a smartphone from this shop.
rows.solution:
Let \(E_1\), \(E_2\) and \(E_3\) be the events that the smartphone bought was manufactured by company A, B and C respectively, and let \(D\) be the event that it is defective. The three companies are the shop's only suppliers, so \(E_1\), \(E_2\), \(E_3\) are mutually exclusive and between them exhaust the inventory, which is exactly the setting for the theorem of total probability. From the passage,
\(P(E_1) = 0\cdot25\), \(P(E_2) = 0\cdot35\), \(P(E_3) = 0\cdot40\),
\(P(D|E_1) = 0\cdot05\), \(P(D|E_2) = 0\cdot04\), \(P(D|E_3) = 0\cdot02\).
By the theorem of total probability,
\(P(D) = P(E_1)P(D|E_1) + P(E_2)P(D|E_2) + P(E_3)P(D|E_3)\)
\(= 0\cdot25 \times 0\cdot05 + 0\cdot35 \times 0\cdot04 + 0\cdot40 \times 0\cdot02\)
\(= 0\cdot0125 + 0\cdot0140 + 0\cdot0080 = 0\cdot0345\).
So the probability that the smartphone bought is defective is \(0\cdot0345\), that is \(\frac{69}{2000}\).

rows.stem: What is the probability that this defective smartphone was manufactured by company B ?
rows.context:
A shop selling electronic items sells smartphones of only three reputed companies A, B and C because chances of their manufacturing a defective smartphone are only 5%, 4% and 2% respectively. In his inventory he has 25% smartphones from company A, 35% smartphones from company B and 40% smartphones from company C.

A person buys a smartphone from this shop.
rows.solution:
The smartphone is already known to be defective, and we are asked to work BACKWARDS from that to the company that made it, so this is Bayes' theorem rather than a forward calculation. Keeping the notation of part (i), we want \(P(E_2|D)\):
\(P(E_2|D) = \frac{P(E_2)\,P(D|E_2)}{P(E_1)P(D|E_1) + P(E_2)P(D|E_2) + P(E_3)P(D|E_3)}\).
The numerator is \(0\cdot35 \times 0\cdot04 = 0\cdot0140\), and the denominator is exactly the total probability \(P(D) = 0\cdot0345\) already computed in part (i), so there is nothing new to work out:
\(P(E_2|D) = \frac{0\cdot0140}{0\cdot0345} = \frac{140}{345} = \frac{28}{69}\).
So the probability that the defective smartphone was manufactured by company B is \(\frac{28}{69}\), or about \(0\cdot406\). Note that this is larger than company B's \(35\%\) share of the inventory, because B's defect rate is double that of company C, which holds the largest share.
